history.heading: The age of the great pyramids
history.text:
The Fourth Dynasty is often called the golden age of the Old Kingdom. In a little over a century, its kings turned the stepped tombs of their predecessors into the smooth-sided true pyramid and built the largest stone monuments Egypt would ever raise. It was also a period of relative peace in which trade and expeditions abroad are recorded officially.

The founder, Sneferu, was the most prolific builder of all. Three pyramids are credited to him: the pyramid at Meidum and, at Dahshur, the Bent Pyramid, whose angle changes halfway up, and the Red Pyramid, the first successful true pyramid. Each one shows the builders learning how to make a stable smooth slope.

history.heading: Giza
history.text:
Sneferu's son Khufu moved the royal cemetery to the Giza plateau and built the Great Pyramid, the largest of them all. His son Djedefre built a pyramid further north at Abu Rawash. Khafre returned to Giza for the second pyramid, and the Great Sphinx is usually attributed to his reign; he also left more statues than any other king of the dynasty. Menkaure built the third and smallest of the main Giza pyramids.

The last secure king, Shepseskaf, broke the chain of pyramid building and was buried in a large mastaba tomb at South Saqqara, known today as Mastabat al-Fir'aun.

history.heading: Running the state
history.text:
The king governed through viziers and through nomarchs in the provinces, and many of the highest offices were held by royal princes. Royal women were prominent too: Khentkaus I carried titles and regalia normally reserved for kings, which has led some scholars to suggest that she may have ruled.

Expeditions went to Sinai, Nubia and Libya for copper, stone and labour, and the Red Sea harbour at Wadi al-Jarf linked Egypt with Sinai. Its art ranges from royal statues and reliefs to limestone busts and sphinxes, such as those of Khafre and Hetepheres II. The dynasty ended around 2494 BCE and was followed by the Fifth Dynasty.

history.heading: A new beginning at Itjtawy
history.text:
The Twelfth Dynasty is often seen as the high point of the Middle Kingdom: a period of stability, expansion and unusually well-recorded history. Its founder, Amenemhat I, moved the capital from Thebes to a new city near el-Lisht called Itjtawy, a name meaning "Amenemhat is the one who seizes the Two Lands". He campaigned south as far as the Second Cataract, began a chain of forts in Nubia and renewed diplomatic contact with Byblos.

His son Senusret I probably ruled alongside him for about ten years, a co-regency that helped secure the succession. Senusret I pushed Egyptian control in Nubia towards the Third Cataract, built his pyramid at el-Lisht and worked on temples across Egypt, including Karnak.

history.heading: Peace, farming and fortresses
history.text:
Amenemhat II reigned in peace while trade with Asia, the Mediterranean and Africa flourished; he built his pyramid at Dahshur. Senusret II was the first king to develop the Faiyum basin for farming, with canals and drainage works that turned it into one of the richest regions of Egypt.

Senusret III changed the shape of the state. He sent punitive campaigns into Nubia, built and enlarged massive border fortresses, and reorganised government by replacing the old system of provinces with three large administrative districts, reducing the power of local governors.

history.heading: Classical literature and the end of the dynasty
history.text:
Amenemhat III is remembered for his pyramid at Hawara and its vast mortuary temple, later known as the Labyrinth. The period produced many of the works later Egyptians treated as classics, including the Story of Sinuhe, the Eloquent Peasant, the Prophecy of Neferti and the Instructions of Amenemhat.

Amenemhat IV appears to have died without an heir. He was followed by Sobekneferu, the first woman confirmed to have taken the full titles of king, who reigned for about four years. After her the throne passed to the kings of the Thirteenth Dynasty.

I. Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000): chronology used on this site

history.heading: Liberation and empire
history.text:
The Eighteenth Dynasty opened the New Kingdom. Ahmose I completed the war against the Hyksos rulers of the north, reunited Egypt and ended the Second Intermediate Period. His successors turned victory into empire: under Thutmose I, Egyptian armies reached Carchemish on the Euphrates and Lower Nubia was conquered.

After the short reign of Thutmose II, his widow Hatshepsut first acted as regent for her young stepson Thutmose III and then took the full titles of king, ruling for about two decades. Thutmose III went on to lead the campaigns that gave Egypt its greatest extent, from Kush in the south to the borders of the Hittite world in the north, beginning with his victory at Megiddo.

history.heading: Splendour and revolution
history.text:
Amenhotep III presided over an era of prosperity, international prestige and lavish building; over 250 statues of him are known. His son Amenhotep IV changed his name to Akhenaten, made the sun disc Aten the centre of state religion and built a new capital at Amarna, called Akhetaten.

The experiment did not outlast him. Tutankhaten, probably his son, became king as a child, restored the traditional cults and changed his name to Tutankhamun. He died young after about a decade on the throne.

history.heading: The last kings
history.text:
Tutankhamun was followed by the official Ay, who married his widow Ankhesenamun, and then by the general Horemheb, who set about erasing the memory of the Amarna kings. Many kings of the dynasty were buried in rock-cut tombs in the Valley of the Kings at Thebes.

Horemheb had no surviving children. He chose his vizier Paramessu as heir, who became king as Ramesses I and founded the Nineteenth Dynasty.

sources.label: Wikipedia, "Eighteenth Dynasty of Egypt" (reference work consulted)
I. Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000): chronology used on this site

history.heading: A family of soldiers
history.text: The Nineteenth Dynasty, the first half of the Ramesside period, was founded by Ramesses I, a former vizier whom Horemheb had chosen as his successor. His reign was short. His son Seti I campaigned against the Libyans and the Hittites and briefly took the Syrian city of Kadesh, before settling an informal peace with the Hittite king. The famous king list of Abydos was completed during his reign.

history.heading: Ramesses the Great
history.text:
Ramesses II ruled for about 66 years. In his fifth year he marched on Kadesh, was caught in an ambush and fought his way out, a battle he later celebrated on temple walls across Egypt. Fighting with the Hittites continued for years until, in his 21st year, he concluded a treaty with the Hittite king Hattusili III, the earliest peace treaty whose text survives.

Ramesses built a new capital in the eastern Delta, Pi-Ramesses, and filled Egypt and Nubia with monuments, among them the rock-cut temples of Abu Simbel and his mortuary temple at Thebes, the Ramesseum.

history.heading: Rivalry and decline
history.text:
Ramesses II outlived many of his sons and was succeeded by Merenptah. After him, rivalry inside the royal family weakened the throne: Amenmesse seized power for a few years before Seti II regained it, and Seti II was followed by the young Siptah and then by Queen Twosret, who ruled as king.

Twosret could not hold power amid court conspiracies. She was probably removed by Setnakhte, the founder of the Twentieth Dynasty.

sources.label: Wikipedia, "Nineteenth Dynasty of Egypt" (reference work consulted)
I. Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000): chronology used on this site

history.heading: Kings from Kush
history.text:
The Twenty-fifth Dynasty came from the kingdom of Kush, in what is now northern Sudan, whose religious centre was Napata at the foot of Jebel Barkal. Kashta, sometimes counted as the first king of the dynasty, already had influence in Upper Egypt: his daughter Amenirdis I became God's Wife of Amun at Thebes.

His successor Piye led his army north, defeated the rulers of Middle and Lower Egypt and recorded his campaign on a long hieroglyphic Victory Stela, in which he presents himself as king of the whole country. Piye also enlarged the Temple of Amun at Jebel Barkal and was buried under the oldest known pyramid at el-Kurru.

history.heading: Rulers of the whole Nile Valley
history.text:
Recent evidence suggests that Shebitku reigned before Shabaka, not after him. Under these kings the capital moved to Memphis, and Egypt and Kush were ruled together. Shabaka restored temples, presented himself as a pious servant of Amun and had the Shabaka Stone inscribed with a religious text.

The dynasty deliberately revived the art and inscriptions of the Old and Middle Kingdoms, a movement scholars call archaism, and its kings built the first pyramids in the Nile Valley for many centuries.

history.heading: Taharqa and the Assyrians
history.text:
Taharqa, crowned at Memphis, built at Jebel Barkal, Kawa, Thebes and Karnak. But Assyria was now the great power of the Near East. Taharqa repelled a first Assyrian invasion in 674 BCE; three years later Esarhaddon took Memphis, and further campaigns under Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal reached Thebes. Taharqa withdrew to Nubia, died there and was buried under the largest pyramid at Nuri.

His successor Tantamani briefly regained Egypt as far as Memphis, but the Assyrians returned and sacked Thebes. The Kushite kings withdrew south and continued to rule from Napata and later Meroë, while Psamtik I reunited Egypt under the Twenty-sixth Dynasty.

sources.label: Wikipedia, "Twenty-fifth Dynasty of Egypt" (reference work consulted)
I. Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (Oxford, 2000): chronology used on this site

history.heading: Reunion under Sais
history.text:
The Twenty-sixth Dynasty ruled from Sais in the western Delta, which gives the period its other name: the Saite Period, the beginning of the Late Period. Its founder Psamtik I came to power with Assyrian backing. As Kushite control of Upper Egypt collapsed, he became sole king of the whole country, with the help of Carian and Greek mercenaries sent by his ally Gyges of Lydia.

Psamtik reigned for more than half a century and restored a strong central state. The Saite kings looked back to the art and inscriptions of earlier periods for their models.

history.heading: Between Babylon and the Greek world
history.text:
Psamtik's son Necho II tried to reassert Egyptian power in the Near East after the fall of Nineveh, but his army was defeated by the Babylonians at Carchemish in 605 BCE. Apries also relied on Greek mercenaries to hold off Babylonian attempts on Egypt.

In 570 BCE Apries was deposed by Ahmose II, better known as Amasis. Apries later came back at the head of a Babylonian army but was defeated, and Amasis's forces repelled a Babylonian invasion under Nebuchadnezzar II a few years into his long reign.

history.heading: The Persian conquest
history.text:
Amasis died in 526 BCE, just as the Persian Empire turned towards Egypt. His son Psamtik III had reigned for only about six months when the Persian king Cambyses II invaded, defeated the Egyptian army and captured him in 525 BCE.

The Twenty-sixth Dynasty was the last native dynasty before Egypt became a province of the Persian Empire, ruled by the kings of the Twenty-seventh Dynasty.
